edges: The Iron Age oil works of Ekron arise after the palace economies of the Late Bronze Age fall.
The presses that supply Greek households with oil are the beam presses of Klazomenai and Attica.
Foxhall uses the prize-oil inscription to estimate how many sacred trees Athena’s oil required.
The archon’s levy on the sacred olives is how the prize oil of the Panathenaic games was gathered.
The burned and regrown Acropolis olive is the best-known of the Athenian olive myths.
The unpredictability of the crop is why Foxhall sees household consumption, not export, as the Athenian oil economy.
Hagnias’ thousand trees are a large estate against the few hundred a household’s oil needed.
Both are Greek olive-processing machines, the crusher breaking the fruit and the beam press extracting the oil.
Jerusalem’s Temple and Athens’s Acropolis both ran on sacred oil, in the folio’s comparison.
Early Indian fat rules cover ghee for the sacrifice and animal fats for the sick monk.
Achaya places ghee in both the sacrifice and the frying pan.
The ghani is the press for the mustard and sesame that the Sutra literature records.
Foxhall counts lighting as the largest non-food share of the household oil bill.
Gymnasium and bath oil is the second non-food use in her accounting.
Foxhall argues the sacred value of oil, in Athena’s olives and prizes, is bound up with its status consumption.
Solon’s law is the state measure that makes Attic oil an export staple, though its authenticity is disputed.
The presses of Greece and the spread of the olive westward belong to one expansion of oil farming.
Greek mockery of butter eaters reflects the south’s oil habit that the household oil figures show.
Ghee’s prestige and the early attestations of mustard and sesame oil are the two sides of India’s fat culture in the same texts.
Sesame and mustard are the oil sources the Sutra literature records.
Sesame oil is the oil of both India and Babylon; the two traditions share the crop, as the earlier folio shows.
Herodotus’s Babylon uses sesame oil; Karmir Blur in Urartu pressed it for export.
Sesame’s westward spread continues from Urartu to Greek Macedonia.
Heliopolis’s olive groves for Ra’s lamps and Tekoa’s oil for the Menorah are the same sacred-lamp economy in two kingdoms.
The Delta’s palm farming grows out of the same long record of African oil-palm use that the folio before this one traces to the third millennium BC.
The Greek olive-oil lamp and the Arctic seal-oil lamp are two fuels for the same domestic light.
Egypt’s castor-oil lamps and the Greek olive-oil lamp are two fuels for the same evening light.
The Record of Rites’ eight delicacies and the Zhou Keeper of Victuals show the same court practice, animal fat as the cooking fat.
Lapita’s coconut and nuts and the Niger Delta’s oil palm are two tropical tree-fat economies of the same centuries.
Herodotus is Kiple’s witness for the fat-tailed sheep, as he is Bedigian’s for the Babylonians’ sesame oil.
Sesame in a Zhejiang tomb and in Vedic ritual are the two Asian ends of the sesame story in the same centuries.
Darius’s sesame exports and Herodotus’s oil-of-sesame Babylon are the Persian-period trade seen from two sides.
The Urartian oil workshop precedes the Achaemenid export trade in the same highlands.
